STD-process-review-taste-46.rule: Wire the picker to the fixed behavior contract: number keys 1–N and ←/→ (wrapping) switch variants, R replays, key events are ignored in inputs, textareas, selects, contenteditable or with a modifier held, exactly one item carries data-active and aria-current="true", the choice persists in a 1-based ?v= URL parameter, and every switch or replay re-mounts the variant so its entrance runs again.
STD-process-review-taste-46.why: The contract is fixed regardless of how the harness renders, so flipping, replaying and reloading behave the same in every exploration.

values.keys: 1–N switch; ← / → step (wrapping); R or r replays
values.ignore: focus in INPUT, TEXTAREA, SELECT or contenteditable; metaKey, ctrlKey or altKey held
values.state: exactly one item with data-active and aria-current="true"; highlight slides to it
values.persistence: ?v=2 via history.replaceState, falling back to variant 1
values.re-mount: switching re-mounts the variant; replay re-mounts without switching (standalone: clear the stage, render on the next animation frame; framework: keyed re-mount)
values.markup: <nav class="proto-picker" aria-label="Prototype variants">; highlight and divider aria-hidden="true"; replay button aria-label="Replay animation (R)"

STD-process-review-taste-47.title: Verify every variant before hand-off
STD-process-review-taste-47.rule: Before showing prototype variants, run the harness and flip through every one yourself, confirming each renders, is reachable from the picker, responds to every interaction and leaves the console clean, and screenshot each variant when browser tooling is available.
STD-process-review-taste-47.why: Verification comes before hand-off; no console errors is part of the completion criterion.

STD-process-review-taste-48.title: Hand off honestly, then stop
STD-process-review-taste-48.rule: Hand off prototype variants as a table (#, Variant, Axis, When it's the right choice, Its cost) with one honest line on when each wins and one on what it costs, say where the picker runs and which keys flip it, never pre-pick a favorite in the table, and stop; if asked for your pick, answer from the product's personality and frequency of use, not aesthetics alone.
STD-process-review-taste-48.why: The choice belongs to the person, and the table must name each variant's tradeoff honestly.

values.table: | # | Variant | Axis | When it's the right choice | Its cost |
values.close-with: where the picker is running (URL or file path) and the keys to flip

STD-process-review-taste-49.title: Promote the pick, then clean up
STD-process-review-taste-49.rule: When the person picks a variant, integrate only that one where it belongs following the project's conventions (file layout, naming, token usage) and delete the prototype surface unless they ask to keep it; for another round, keep the harness and diverge around the direction they leaned toward.
STD-process-review-taste-49.why: Promotion ends the exploration and cleans up after the choice; a new round refines toward what the person gravitated to.

values.keep <variant>: promote and delete the prototype surface
values.riff <variant>: new round diverging around that direction

STD-process-review-taste-50.title: Working is not finished
STD-process-review-taste-50.rule: Do not treat a product that merely works as finished: invest in its look and feel, good defaults and good animations, and go the extra mile rather than ship something mediocre.
STD-process-review-taste-50.why: Everyone can ship something that works, especially with AI, and people expect things to work; what makes a product stand out is brand, design, intuitiveness and the overall experience, and beauty is underused in software, so it is leverage.

STD-process-review-taste-51.title: Train taste on the best work
STD-process-review-taste-51.rule: Build a curated list of respected tastemakers (and the people they admire), study their designs, apps and books, and reverse-engineer the animations and interactions of the best interfaces instead of stopping once your UI works.
STD-process-review-taste-51.why: Good taste is a trained instinct, not personal preference; exposure to great work teaches how greatness looks and feels, and learning from the best is the best way to learn.

STD-process-review-taste-52.title: Say why it feels right
STD-process-review-taste-52.rule: When judging design or motion, explain why something feels great or wrong and name the pattern behind it, instead of labelling it good or bad or trusting gut feel alone.
STD-process-review-taste-52.why: Rationalising builds taste, and almost every taste decision has a logical reason if you look close enough; putting it into words trains the ability to articulate judgement, which is valuable in the AI era.

STD-process-review-taste-53.title: Practise the craft and seek critique
STD-process-review-taste-53.rule: Practise by making things, ask the right person for critique while you do, and keep going when early work falls short of your own standard.
STD-process-review-taste-53.why: Practice makes you a good judge of taste and, in time, a tastemaker; good critique accelerates learning more than trial and error alone, and early work falling short means your taste is ahead of your skill.

STD-process-review-taste-54.title: Train judgement with side-by-side pairs
STD-process-review-taste-54.rule: Train motion judgement by comparing two versions of the same animation side by side, picking the better one and writing down why before reading an expert breakdown, so you learn to spot what is wrong, name it and fix it.
STD-process-review-taste-54.why: This trains the ability to spot what's wrong, name it, and fix it, which AI cannot do for you.

values.method: two animations side by side; pick the better one; write down why; then compare with the breakdown

STD-process-review-taste-55.title: Give agents strict rules with reasons
STD-process-review-taste-55.rule: Package taste for coding agents as written rule files, one per aspect of the interface, where every rule is strict and states why it has to be done that way, and give them to agents before asking for UI or motion work.
STD-process-review-taste-55.why: Agents don't know what great feels like for visual work; strict rules with their reasons mean the agent doesn't guess or make up its own rules, the way you would guide a less experienced designer.

values.aspects: e.g. animation, layout, icons, color theory, typography

STD-process-review-taste-56.title: Understand the motion code AI writes
STD-process-review-taste-56.rule: Make sure whoever ships animation code understands how it works, even when a model wrote it, and use AI to amplify real design or engineering expertise, not to replace it.
STD-process-review-taste-56.why: People who clearly understand the code will be even more leveraged; AI doesn't replace domain expertise, it amplifies what you can get out of it.

STD-process-review-taste-57.title: Name the effect when prompting
STD-process-review-taste-57.rule: When asking an AI or a designer for a motion effect, name it with its exact term (for example Stagger, Pop in, Rubber-banding, Origin-aware animation) rather than a vague description.
STD-process-review-taste-57.why: Using the right words gets better animations from an AI.

values.lookup: the animation-vocabulary glossary (Entrances & Exits, Sequencing & Timing, Movement & Transforms, Transitions Between States, Scroll, Feedback & Interaction, Easing, Spring Animations, Looping & Ambient Motion, Polish & Effects, Performance, Principles to Know)

STD-process-review-taste-58.title: Answer naming questions from the glossary
STD-process-review-taste-58.rule: Answer 'what is it called' motion questions by mapping what the person sees or feels to a glossary term, quoting its description verbatim as '**Term** — description', listing 1–2 close alternates with how each differs when several fit, saying plainly when a match is only an approximation, and never inventing a term.
STD-process-review-taste-58.why: People describe what they see or feel, not the technical name; the glossary's descriptions are authoritative, and a naming question wants a name, not an essay.

values.alternates: best match first, then 1–2 under 'Close alternates:' with a one-line note on how each differs
values.no-match: name the closest term and say it's an approximation, or combine glossary terms (e.g. 'a stagger of scale-in entrances')

STD-process-review-taste-59.title: Teach motion with demos people can touch
STD-process-review-taste-59.rule: When teaching or explaining motion, let people play with interactive demos, including bad-versus-good examples, rather than explaining it in text alone.
STD-process-review-taste-59.why: People need to feel the difference between good and bad, and the only way is to experience it themselves, like touching a physical object to understand its texture; nobody wants to read a dry wall of text about something this visual.

STD-process-review-taste-60.title: Documentation is part of the product
STD-process-review-taste-60.rule: Write documentation and clear instructions as part of the work, not as an afterthought, with interactive examples people can play with and ready-to-use code snippets.
STD-process-review-taste-60.why: Good documentation drastically lowers the barrier to using any product, yet it is often overlooked; interactive examples let people understand the product before they use it.

STD-process-review-taste-62.title: Auto-save work in progress
STD-process-review-taste-62.rule: Save work in built-in editors and exercises automatically, so stopping midway loses nothing.
STD-process-review-taste-62.why: If you stop in the middle of an exercise, your progress won't be lost.

STD-process-review-taste-63.title: Keep the product alive with a changelog
STD-process-review-taste-63.rule: Keep shipping updates to a product and refresh existing parts as you learn better ways, and record every update on a changelog page.
STD-process-review-taste-63.why: A product that keeps evolving doesn't die out as a snapshot in time; the changelog documents all the updates.

STD-process-review-taste-64.title: Talk the animation through before coding
STD-process-review-taste-64.rule: Plan an animation by thinking and talking through what it should do before writing code, then code it, improve it and iterate.
STD-process-review-taste-64.why: This is the author's exact process in his walkthroughs, shown so learners see the reasons behind each decision.

STD-process-review-taste-65.title: Learn CSS animation before Motion
STD-process-review-taste-65.rule: Get the basics of CSS animation (transforms, transitions, keyframe animations) right, and know when and how to use each, before reaching for Motion (Framer Motion).
STD-process-review-taste-65.why: With the CSS basics right you can transition into Framer Motion with ease.

STD-process-review-taste-66.title: Don't tease unfinished work
STD-process-review-taste-66.rule: Do not publicly tease a project before it is done; if you need outside pressure to finish, commit to something concrete such as a public deadline instead.
STD-process-review-taste-66.why: Teasing ui.land made finishing less motivating because talking about it already felt rewarding (teased in December 2021, launched January 2023); a presale with a public deadline forced the work.

STD-process-review-taste-67.title: The first screen after sign-up sets the tone
STD-process-review-taste-67.rule: Treat the first screen people land on after signing up or enrolling as part of the product's packaging: design it to set the tone and show the care people can expect from the rest of the product.
STD-process-review-taste-67.why: Onboarding is the first impression of the product itself; the course's welcome page with a customizable 'Motion Passport' sets the tone and shows the care to expect from the rest of the content. It is a rare, first-time moment, where delight motion is allowed (STD-when-to-animate-09).
